sections.text:
Ismail, peace be upon him, is the firstborn son and the great gift bestowed upon Abraham Al-Khalil after many years of waiting and patience.

Ishmael was born to Mrs. Hagar, Abraham's wife, and he was the joy of his father's heart, who had reached an old age without having a son.

But God wanted to put Abraham to a great test, so he ordered him to take his wife Hagar and his infant Ishmael and leave them in a desolate valley with no crops or water.

Abraham obeyed the command of his Lord, and brought them to the site of the Holy Kaaba in Mecca, and left them there with a few dates and a jug of water.

Hajar said with the certainty of a believer: “Has God commanded you to do this?” When he answered her in the affirmative, she said with a reassured heart: “Then He will not waste us.”

The water ran out after a short time, and Ismail began crying from extreme thirst, and his mother started running between the mountains of Safa and Marwa, searching for any caravan or a drop of water.

After she had worked seven laps while she was extremely tired and desperate, divine relief came.

Gabriel, peace be upon him, hit the ground with his wing (or Ishmael hit the ground with his little foot), and the pure and blessed spring of Zamzam water exploded from under his feet.

They drank and drank, and thanks to this water, birds began to fly over the place, which attracted the Arab “Jarham” tribe, who asked Hagar for permission to live with them.

Ismail grew up in Mecca and learned classical Arabic from the Jarhum tribe. He was trained in archery and horsemanship until he became one of the most skilled knights.

When Ismail grew up and began to accompany his father in his work, the greatest test came.

Abraham saw in a dream that he was slaughtering his son, and the vision of the prophets was a revelation and an order from God that must be implemented.

Ibrahim went to his son and presented the matter to him, saying: “My son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you see.”

The righteous and obedient Ismail answered with all courage and submission to God’s command: “O my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, God willing, among those who are patient.”

When Abraham put the knife on his son's neck in submission to God, God called Abraham that the vision had come true.

May God redeem him with a great ram that he sent down from heaven, and this great event became the basis of the Eid al-Adha sacrifice that Muslims celebrate every year in commemoration of this great sacrifice.

Ismail grew up and married from the Jarham tribe, and he was kind to his father Ibrahim and visited him from time to time.

During one visit, Abraham told his son that God had commanded him to build a house of worship in Mecca.

The father and son began to build the Holy Kaaba. Ismail was collecting stones, and Abraham was building, and they prayed to God: “Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed, You are the Hearer, the Knower.”

When the building rose, Abraham stood on a stone now known as “the Maqam of Abraham,” and completed the construction of the Kaaba to be a qibla for the monotheists.

God sent Ishmael as a prophet and messenger to the tribes of Yemen and the Amalekites who lived in the Hijaz, so he called them to monotheism, to perform prayer, and to pay zakat.

God described him in the Qur’an as being true to his promise, commanding his family to pray and pay zakat, and being pleasing to his Lord.

From the descendants of Ishmael, peace be upon him, the Mozarabic Arabs spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

God honored this pure lineage by choosing from them the Seal of the Prophets and Messengers, Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace.

The moral of the story is the virtue of honoring one’s parents and absolute submission to God’s commands, even if they are against one’s whims, and that patience in the face of calamity is followed by relief and honor.
